A **coaxal system** is a family of circles sharing a common radical axis. Here the family is
x² + y² + 2gx + c = 0, with **g** the parameter that varies and **c** fixed and negative.
**Step 1 — find the centre and radius of a typical member.**
centre = **(−g, 0)** — every centre lies on the x-axis
radius = √(g² − c)
**Step 2 — check the circles are real.** Since c < 0, we have −c > 0, so
g² − c = g² + |c| > 0 **for every g**
Every member is therefore a genuine circle, never a point and never imaginary.
**Step 3 — look for common points.** Set x = 0 in the equation; the term 2gx vanishes, so
whatever g is:
y² + c = 0
y² = −c
**y = ±√(−c)**
which is real because c < 0. So **every** circle in the family passes through the two fixed
points
**(0, √(−c))** and **(0, −√(−c))**
**Step 4 — conclude.** All the circles meet one another at these same two points, so the
system consists of **intersecting circles** ✓
**The contrast with c > 0.** Then y² = −c has no real solution, the circles share no common
point, and the system is the **non-intersecting** type — option (2) — which also possesses
two **limiting points** at (±√c, 0), the degenerate members of zero radius. For c < 0 the
radius g² − c never reaches zero, so there are no limiting points at all.
**The dividing case c = 0** gives x² + y² + 2gx = 0, every member passing through the origin
and tangent to the y-axis there — the **touching** system, option (3).
So the single number c decides the character of the whole family:
**c < 0** → intersecting, through two real common points
**c = 0** → touching at the origin
**c > 0** → non-intersecting, with two limiting points
∴ intersecting circles.

The **director circle** of a conic is the locus of points from which **two perpendicular
tangents** can be drawn to it.
**Step 1 — recall the result.** For the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, the director circle is
**x² + y² = a² − b²**
(For the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 it is x² + y² = a² + b², with a **plus** — the sign
follows the sign in the conic's own equation, which makes the pair easy to remember.)
**Step 2 — read off a² and b².** Comparing x²/16 − y²/4 = 1 with the standard form:
**a² = 16** and **b² = 4**
**Step 3 — substitute.**
x² + y² = 16 − 4 = **12**
so the director circle is **x² + y² = 12** ✓ of radius 2√3 ≈ 3·46.
**Where the result comes from.** A line y = mx + c is tangent to the hyperbola when
c² = a²m² − b². Two such tangents through a point (h, k) are perpendicular when their
gradients satisfy m₁m₂ = −1. Writing c = k − mh and substituting gives a quadratic in m:
(h² − a²)m² − 2hkm + (k² + b²) = 0
whose product of roots is (k² + b²)/(h² − a²). Setting that equal to −1:
k² + b² = −h² + a² ⟹ **h² + k² = a² − b²** ✓
**Why the condition a² > b² matters.** The radius² is a² − b², so a real director circle
exists only when **a² > b²**. Here 16 > 4 ✓ so the circle is genuine. Had b² exceeded a²,
no point would admit two perpendicular tangents at all.
**The distractors** are each a plausible mis-remembering: **16** uses a² alone, **4** uses b²
alone, and **20** uses a² + b² — the **ellipse** formula applied to a hyperbola, which is
the single likeliest error.
∴ x² + y² = 12.

equals the radius. Since the centre is given, that distance **is** the radius.

= |5| / √25

A quotient of five complex factors is far quicker in **polar form**, where multiplying adds
the arguments and dividing subtracts them. The question asks only *where* the result lies,
so only the **argument** matters.
**Step 1 — put each factor into modulus–argument form.**
**−√3 + 3i:** modulus √(3 + 9) = √12 = **2√3**. The point is in the second quadrant, with
reference angle arctan(3/√3) = arctan √3 = 60°, so arg = 180° − 60° = **120°**
**1 − i:** modulus √2, fourth quadrant, arg = **−45°**
**3 + √3 i:** modulus √(9 + 3) = **2√3**, first quadrant, arg = arctan(√3/3) = arctan(1/√3)
= **30°**
**i:** modulus 1, arg = **90°**
**√3 + √3 i:** modulus √(3 + 3) = **√6**, first quadrant, equal parts so arg = **45°**
**Step 2 — combine the numerator.**
modulus = 2√3 × √2 = **2√6**
argument = 120° + (−45°) = **75°**
**Step 3 — combine the denominator.**
modulus = 2√3 × 1 × √6 = 2√18 = **6√2**
argument = 30° + 90° + 45° = **165°**
**Step 4 — divide.**
modulus = 2√6/(6√2) = (1/3)√3 = **1/√3**
argument = 75° − 165° = **−90°**
**Step 5 — read off the position.** An argument of −90° points straight **down** the
imaginary axis, so the number is
z = (1/√3)(cos(−90°) + i sin(−90°)) = **−i/√3**
It is **purely imaginary**, so it lies **on the Y-axis (imaginary axis)** ✓
**Check by direct multiplication.**
numerator: (−√3 + 3i)(1 − i) = −√3 + √3 i + 3i − 3i² = (3 − √3) + (3 + √3)i ≈ 1·27 + 4·73i
denominator: (3 + √3 i)(i) = −√3 + 3i, and then
(−√3 + 3i)(√3 + √3 i) = −3 − 3i + 3√3 i + 3√3 i² = (−3 − 3√3) + (3√3 − 3)i ≈ −8·20 + 2·20i
Dividing, z ≈ (1·27 + 4·73i)/(−8·20 + 2·20i) ≈ **−0·577i** ✓ and 1/√3 ≈ 0·577 ✓ with the
real part vanishing to rounding error.
**Why polar form is the right tool here.** The direct route needs four multiplications of
binomials and a rationalisation; the polar route needs five arctangents that are all
standard angles — 120°, −45°, 30°, 90°, 45° — and then two additions. The question is built
from angles that sum to a multiple of 90°, which is the signal that it was designed for the
polar method.
∴ on the Y-axis (imaginary axis).

Simplify the number first, then conjugate it — doing it the other way round is more work.
**Step 1 — expand the numerator.**
(1 + i)² = 1 + 2i + i² = 1 + 2i − 1 = **2i**
This is worth memorising: **(1 + i)² = 2i** and **(1 − i)² = −2i**.
**Step 2 — divide.**
z = 2i/(1 − i)
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, 1 + i:
z = 2i(1 + i) / [(1 − i)(1 + i)]
numerator: 2i + 2i² = 2i − 2 = **−2 + 2i**
denominator: 1² + 1² = **2**
z = (−2 + 2i)/2 = **−1 + i**
**Step 3 — take the conjugate**, which flips the sign of the imaginary part only:
z̄ = **−1 − i** ✓
**Check in polar form.** 1 + i = √2 ∠45°, so (1 + i)² = 2 ∠90°, and 1 − i = √2 ∠−45°.
Dividing: modulus 2/√2 = √2, argument 90° − (−45°) = **135°**
z = √2 ∠135° = √2(−1/√2 + i/√2) = **−1 + i** ✓
and the conjugate reflects it in the real axis, to √2 ∠−135° = **−1 − i** ✓
**The trap.** Option (4), −1 + i, is **z itself** — the answer you get by simplifying
correctly and then forgetting to conjugate at the last step. Since the question's only real
work is the simplification, it is easy to feel finished one step early. The conjugate must
have the **opposite** sign on its i.
∴ −1 − i.

Note: the printed key gives the fourth option, −1 + i. That is the number itself, not its
conjugate: the working above gives z = −1 + i and hence z̄ = −1 − i, the third option. The
key has been corrected.

With A = [[3, 2], [1, 1]], the relation A² + xA + yI = 0 is the matrix's **characteristic
equation**, and the Cayley–Hamilton theorem supplies x and y directly from the trace and
the determinant.
**Step 1 — find the trace and determinant.**
trace = 3 + 1 = **4** (the sum of the leading diagonal)
determinant = (3)(1) − (2)(1) = 3 − 2 = **1**
**Step 2 — write the characteristic equation.** For any 2×2 matrix,
A² − (trace)A + (det)I = 0
so here
A² − 4A + I = 0
**Step 3 — compare with A² + xA + yI = 0.**
**x = −4** and **y = 1**, so **(x, y) = (−4, 1)** ✓
**Verification by direct computation**, which is worth doing once to see the theorem work.
A² = [[3, 2], [1, 1]] × [[3, 2], [1, 1]]
top-left: (3)(3) + (2)(1) = 9 + 2 = **11**
top-right: (3)(2) + (2)(1) = 6 + 2 = **8**
bottom-left: (1)(3) + (1)(1) = 3 + 1 = **4**
bottom-right: (1)(2) + (1)(1) = 2 + 1 = **3**
A² = [[11, 8], [4, 3]]
Now form A² − 4A + I:
[[11, 8], [4, 3]] − [[12, 8], [4, 4]] + [[1, 0], [0, 1]]
top-left: 11 − 12 + 1 = **0**
top-right: 8 − 8 + 0 = **0**
bottom-left: 4 − 4 + 0 = **0**
bottom-right: 3 − 4 + 1 = **0**
= the zero matrix ✓
**The sign trap.** The theorem has a **minus** before the trace, so x is **−4**, not +4.
Option (1), (4, −1), has both signs flipped — the answer obtained by writing
A² + (trace)A − (det)I = 0 from memory. Checking against the zero matrix, as above, settles
it in a few lines.
**Why this is useful beyond the question.** Rearranging A² = 4A − I lets any power of A be
written in terms of A and I without ever multiplying matrices again — A³ = 4A² − A
= 4(4A − I) − A = 15A − 4I, and so on. Multiplying through by A⁻¹ instead gives
A⁻¹ = 4I − A, an inverse found with no division at all.
∴ (−4, 1).
